# Exercise 2.3 — Exploring and cleaning messy patient data {#sec-cleaning}


## Overview

Real data is messy! If done properly, most of the time in a data anlysis project is spent understanding the data, cleaning it and preprocessing it to the format you require for downstream analysis. Messiness comes in many different ways so just be aware that you need to visualize, ask questions and practice! Below you have some common examples you might encounter as well as some inisght into what one-hot encoding means. 


## The data

`messy_gp_patients.csv` holds 30 patients from a handful of GP practices, with
their age, height and smoking status.

[**Download `messy_gp_patients.csv`**](data/messy_gp_patients.csv){download="messy_gp_patients.csv"} and save it in your `data` folder,
or take every file at once from the zip on the [introduction page](index.qmd).

:::::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

### 1. First look at the data

Load it and look before you touch anything.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(tidyverse)
library(fastDummies)

gp <- read_csv("data/messy_gp_patients.csv")

glimpse(gp)
summary(gp)
```


::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Think about it
1. How many patients and how many variables are there?
2. Which columns came in as numbers and which as text?
3. Does anything look wrong? 
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
Thirty patients, five variables.

`age` arrived as a number and `height_cm` as **text**, which is the first
finding. A column of heights should be numeric; it is not, so something in it is
not a number. One text value anywhere in a column is enough to make the whole
column text.

`summary()` then shows an age of 250, which no patient has and minimum height of 1.5 cm
:::
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2. Cleaning the numerical variables

#### Height

Look at what is actually in the column:

```{r}
unique(gp$height_cm)
```

Two values are not ordinary heights in centimetres: `unknown`, and `1.72` —
a height recorded in metres. 

```{r}
gp <- gp |>
  mutate(
    height_cm = na_if(height_cm, "unknown"), #what is this function doing? Check it out!!  https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/na_if.html
    height_cm = as.numeric(height_cm), # why do we have to have this after the NA has been corrected? 
    height_cm = if_else(!is.na(height_cm) & height_cm < 3, # what re we doing here?  
                        height_cm * 100,
                        height_cm)
  )

summary(gp$height_cm)
```

Heights now run from 155 to 183 cm, with one missing.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Important

This process of turning messy data into clean structured format is called *data wrangling* and the best way to get better at it is lots of practice. Tidyverse has developed a language to help you do this in a consistent way. Practice and explore the functions available to you. The more you use them, the more you will understand how to use them effectively. To discover what is available explore, for example here are amazing examples of data wrnagling at their best by the same people taht develop tidyverse  [Tidy Tuesday](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL19ev-r1GBwkuyiwnxoHTRC8TTqP8OEi8)  
:::

Lets continue. We detected a possibe data entry error with age of 250 through summarise. Would have also detected it through a boxplot. 

#### Age

Find the implausible ones rather than assuming you know where they are:

```{r}

ggplot(gp, aes(y = age)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(y = "Age (years)") + 
  theme_bw()


```

With the following filter we can set implausible values to `NA`
```{r}
gp <- gp |>
  mutate(age = if_else(age < 0 | age > 110, NA_real_, as.numeric(age)))

sum(is.na(gp$age))
```

One patient, P014, recorded at 250.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Think about it
Why is replacing an impossible age with missing better than replacing it with
zero — or than leaving it at 250?
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3. Exploring and collapsing the GP practices

How many patients are registered at each practice?

```{r}
gp |> count(GP_practice, sort = TRUE)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## From characters to factors

GP practice is currently stored as a character variable. However, it represents a set of distinct categories rather than free text.

In R, we can represent categorical variables using factors.

```{r}
class(gp$GP_practice)

```

```{r}
gp <- gp |>
  mutate(GP_practice = factor(GP_practice))

```

```{r}
class(gp$GP_practice)
levels(gp$GP_practice)
```

Explore more about factors [r4ds] (https://r4ds.hadley.nz/factors.html) 

:::




```{r}
#| fig-height: 2.6
gp |>
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_infreq(GP_practice))) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = "GP practice", y = "Number of patients")
```

Three practices have a single patient. Difficult to establish any association with it (cannot find a pattern if just one sample! )so lets combine anything with fewer than three patients into an `Other` category:

```{r}
gp <- gp |>
  mutate(GP_practice = fct_lump_min(factor(GP_practice),
                                    min = 3,
                                    other_level = "Other"))

gp |> count(GP_practice, sort = TRUE)
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Think about it
1. How many practices were there to begin with, and how many are left?
2. Where did the three single-patient practices go — and look carefully, because
   the answer is not "into a new category".
3. What information did you just lose?
:::


------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4. Cleaning and visualising smoking status

Count the categories as recorded:

```{r}
gp |> count(smoking_status, sort = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 2.6
gp |>
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_infreq(smoking_status))) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = "Smoking status", y = "Patients")
```

Ten different spellings for what are really three categories, plus two codes
that mean "not recorded". Standardise the labels and turn the codes into
missing values:

```{r}
gp <- gp |>
  mutate(
    smoking_status = str_to_lower(str_trim(smoking_status)),
    smoking_status = case_when(
      smoking_status %in% c("never", "non-smoker", "non smoker") ~ "Never",
      smoking_status %in% c("former", "ex-smoker", "ex smoker")  ~ "Former",
      smoking_status %in% c("current", "current smoker", "smoker") ~ "Current",
      smoking_status %in% c("unknown", "n/a", "", "?") ~ NA_character_,
      TRUE ~ smoking_status
    ),
    smoking_status = factor(smoking_status)
  )

gp |> count(smoking_status, sort = TRUE)
```

Never 12, Former 8, Current 7, and 3 genuinely missing.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Think about it
1. Why standardise the labels *before* encoding or analysing them? Understand what each function does! They will get more intuitive with practice and always be in the lookout for easier ways of performing your analysis! Instead of using this case_when could have done long ifelse statements but this is more readable and easier to understand.
2. `Never` and `never` differed by one capital letter. What would a model have
   done with them?
:::



------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 5. What happens when you one-hot encode?

Most algorithms need numbers, so a categorical variable has to become numeric
somehow. One-hot encoding gives each category its own 0/1 column.

```{r}
gp_encoded <- dummy_cols(gp,
                         select_columns = "GP_practice",
                         remove_selected_columns = TRUE) #why is this important? 

ncol(gp)
ncol(gp_encoded)
# View(gp_encoded)
```

Five columns became nine: the practice column is gone and five indicator
columns have taken its place.

Now try the same thing on the patient identifier:

```{r}
gp_ids_encoded <- dummy_cols(gp,
                             select_columns = "patient_id",
                             remove_selected_columns = TRUE)

c(original = ncol(gp),
  practice_encoded = ncol(gp_encoded),
  id_encoded = ncol(gp_ids_encoded))
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Think about it
1. How many columns did each encoding add?
2. What do the 0 (cold) and the 1 (hot) actually mean?
3. Why was collapsing the rare practices worth doing *before* encoding?
5. Should every categorical variable be one-hot encoded? What do you think of a gender column with just Male and Female class? Should we hot-encode it? 
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
Encoding the practice took 5 columns to 9 — one column out, five in. Encoding
the identifier took 5 to 34: one column out, thirty in, one per patient.

A 1 means "this patient is at this practice" and a 0 means "is not". For the
identifier, each column is 1 for exactly one person and 0 for the other
twenty-nine, so it can only ever identify that individual. On a real extract of
50,000 patients it would produce 50,000 columns, and not one of them would
apply to patient 50,001 — the only patient you actually care about predicting.

Collapsing first is what kept the practice encoding at five columns rather than
eight, with every column backed by at least three patients. A column with one
patient in it cannot support an estimate of anything; it can only be memorised.

So no. Being categorical does not make a variable worth encoding. Decide what a
variable *means* — identifier, group, measurement — before deciding what to do
with it.
:::
:::

## Python

### 1. First look at the data

Load it and look before you touch anything.

```{python}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

gp_py = pd.read_csv("data/messy_gp_patients.csv",
                    keep_default_na=False, na_values=[""])

print(gp_py.shape)
print(gp_py.dtypes)
print(gp_py.describe(include="all"))
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Why those two arguments
`pandas` treats `N/A`, `NA`, `null` and `NaN` as missing the moment it reads a
file. Here that would quietly convert one of the smoking-status codes before you
ever saw it, and spotting those codes is part of the exercise.
`keep_default_na=False` switches that off; `na_values=[""]` keeps genuinely
empty cells missing.
:::

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Think about it
1. How many patients and how many variables are there?
2. Which columns came in as numbers and which as text?
3. Does anything look wrong with `height_cm` or `age`?
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
Thirty patients, five variables.

`age` arrived as `int64` and `height_cm` as `object` — `pandas` for text —
which is the first finding. A column of heights should be numeric; it is not, so
something in it is not a number. One text value anywhere in a column is enough
to make the whole column text.

`describe()` then shows an age of 250, which no patient has.
:::
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2. Cleaning the numerical variables

#### Height

Look at what is actually in the column:

```{python}
print(gp_py["height_cm"].unique())
```

Two values are not ordinary heights in centimetres: `unknown`, and `1.72` —
a height recorded in metres. They need different treatment, because one of them
is recoverable and the other is not.

```{python}
gp_py["height_cm"] = pd.to_numeric(
    gp_py["height_cm"].replace("unknown", np.nan), errors="coerce")

gp_py.loc[gp_py["height_cm"] < 3, "height_cm"] *= 100

print(gp_py["height_cm"].describe().round(1))
```

Heights now run from 155 to 183 cm, with one missing.

#### Age

Find the implausible ones rather than assuming you know where they are:

```{python}
print(gp_py[(gp_py["age"] < 0) | (gp_py["age"] > 110)])
```

```{python}
gp_py["age"] = gp_py["age"].where((gp_py["age"] >= 0) & (gp_py["age"] <= 110))

print(int(gp_py["age"].isna().sum()))
```

One patient, P014, recorded at 250.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Think about it
Why is replacing an impossible age with missing better than replacing it with
zero — or than leaving it at 250?
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
Because 0 is a number a model will believe. It would be treated as a newborn,
pulling the mean age down and the age–outcome relationship with it. Leaving 250
is worse again, for the same reason in the other direction.

Missing is the only one of the three that is *true*. We know the recorded value
is wrong and we do not know what it should have been — it could have been 25, or
50, or a mistyped date of birth. Missing says exactly that, and every later step
can then decide what to do about it. Note the contrast with the height in
metres: `1.72` could only have meant `172`, so that one is corrected rather than
discarded. Correcting a value you can infer is cleaning; inventing one you
cannot is something else.
:::
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3. Exploring and collapsing the GP practices

How many patients are registered at each practice?

```{python}
print(gp_py["GP_practice"].value_counts())
```

```{python}
#| fig-height: 2.6
counts = gp_py["GP_practice"].value_counts()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 2.6))
ax.barh(counts.index[::-1], counts.values[::-1], color="steelblue")
ax.set_xlabel("Number of patients")
ax.set_ylabel("GP practice")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Three practices have a single patient. Combine anything with fewer than three
into an `Other` category:

```{python}
counts = gp_py["GP_practice"].value_counts()
rare = counts[counts < 3].index

gp_py["GP_practice"] = gp_py["GP_practice"].where(
    ~gp_py["GP_practice"].isin(rare), "Other")

print(gp_py["GP_practice"].value_counts())
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Think about it
1. How many practices were there to begin with, and how many are left?
2. Where did the three single-patient practices go — and look carefully, because
   the answer is not "into a new category".
3. What information did you just lose?
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
Eight practices become five: Bournbrook 9, Cherry Tree 7, Dovecote Lane 6,
Selly Oak 3, and `Other` 5.

The extract **already had** an `Other` category with two patients, and
Harborne, Edgbaston and Kings Heath were merged into it rather than into a
second one. Two plus three is the five you see. That is worth checking every
time you group rare levels, because an `Other` that already exists and an
`Other` you create mean different things and will be silently combined.

What you lose is the identity of those three practices. If one of them had an
unusual case mix — a practice serving a care home, say — that signal is now
averaged into a category whose only shared property is being small. What you
gain is five columns instead of eight when you encode, each supported by at
least three patients.
:::
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4. Cleaning and visualising smoking status

Count the categories as recorded:

```{python}
print(gp_py["smoking_status"].value_counts(dropna=False))
```

```{python}
#| fig-height: 2.6
counts = gp_py["smoking_status"].value_counts(dropna=False)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 2.6))
ax.barh([str(i) for i in counts.index][::-1], counts.values[::-1],
        color="steelblue")
ax.set_xlabel("Patients")
ax.set_ylabel("Smoking status")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Ten different spellings for what are really three categories, plus two codes
that mean "not recorded". Standardise the labels and turn the codes into
missing values:

```{python}
spelling = gp_py["smoking_status"].str.strip().str.lower()

labels = {**{k: "Never"   for k in ["never", "non-smoker", "non smoker"]},
          **{k: "Former"  for k in ["former", "ex-smoker", "ex smoker"]},
          **{k: "Current" for k in ["current", "current smoker", "smoker"]},
          **{k: np.nan    for k in ["unknown", "n/a", "", "?"]}}

gp_py["smoking_status"] = spelling.map(labels)

print(gp_py["smoking_status"].value_counts(dropna=False))
```

Never 12, Former 8, Current 7, and 3 genuinely missing.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Think about it
1. Why standardise the labels *before* encoding or analysing them?
2. `Never` and `never` differed by one capital letter. What would a model have
   done with them?
3. The recipe above lower-cases and trims **before** matching. Why is that order
   necessary rather than tidy?
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
Because a category is only a category if it is spelled one way. Left alone,
`Never` and `never` are two different values: a frequency table reports 8 and 4
instead of 12, a bar chart shows two bars, and one-hot encoding produces two
columns — each with a smaller count than the real category, so each looks rarer
and weaker than it is. The model never learns they are the same thing; it
cannot, because nothing in the data says so.

Lower-casing and trimming first turns `Never`, `never` and a stray
` never ` into one string before any matching happens. Match first and you would
need an entry for every spelling, and you would miss the one you did not think
of. Cleaning the form of a value and then matching on meaning is the order that
scales.
:::
:::

### 5. What happens when you one-hot encode?

Most algorithms need numbers, so a categorical variable has to become numeric
somehow. One-hot encoding gives each category its own 0/1 column.

```{python}
gp_encoded = pd.get_dummies(gp_py, columns=["GP_practice"], dtype=int)

print(gp_py.shape[1])
print(gp_encoded.shape[1])

cols = ["patient_id"] + [c for c in gp_encoded.columns
                         if c.startswith("GP_practice_")]
print(gp_encoded[cols].head(10))
```

Five columns became nine: the practice column is gone and five indicator
columns have taken its place.

Now try the same thing on the patient identifier:

```{python}
gp_ids_encoded = pd.get_dummies(gp_py, columns=["patient_id"], dtype=int)

print({"original": gp_py.shape[1],
       "practice_encoded": gp_encoded.shape[1],
       "id_encoded": gp_ids_encoded.shape[1]})
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Think about it
1. How many columns did each encoding add?
2. What do the 0 and the 1 actually mean?
3. Why was collapsing the rare practices worth doing *before* encoding?
4. Would the patient-identifier columns help predict anything about a patient
   who is not in this table?
5. So: should every categorical variable be one-hot encoded?
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
Encoding the practice took 5 columns to 9 — one column out, five in. Encoding
the identifier took 5 to 34: one column out, thirty in, one per patient.

A 1 means "this patient is at this practice" and a 0 means "is not". For the
identifier, each column is 1 for exactly one person and 0 for the other
twenty-nine, so it can only ever identify that individual. On a real extract of
50,000 patients it would produce 50,000 columns, and not one of them would
apply to patient 50,001 — the only patient you actually care about predicting.

Collapsing first is what kept the practice encoding at five columns rather than
eight, with every column backed by at least three patients. A column with one
patient in it cannot support an estimate of anything; it can only be memorised.

So no. Being categorical does not make a variable worth encoding. Decide what a
variable *means* — identifier, group, measurement — before deciding what to do
with it.
:::
:::
